slides.say: Now a new question. A B is a diameter of a circle with radius nine. Six identical smaller circles have their centers on A B. Their diameters cover A B from end to end. What is the sum of the circumferences of the six smaller circles?
So we need the six small circumferences, all added together. We'll solve it in two different ways.
Let's start with the math way. The big radius is nine, so the diameter A B is two times nine, eighteen.
Six small diameters fill A B. So each small diameter is eighteen divided by six, three.
at: Six small diameters fill A B

slides.say: A radius is half a diameter. So the small radius is three divided by two, one and a half.

slides: Honestly, a radius of one and a half is a bit annoying. It's a fraction. But we can still calculate. The circumference is two pi r.

slides.say: Two times one and a half is three. So one small circumference is three pi.
at: Two times one and a half

slides.say: There are six of them. Six times three pi is eighteen pi. Now let's see a faster way, with no annoying radius.
Now by understanding, with similarity. All circles are similar to each other.
Let's call the small radius r. The big diameter is six small diameters. So the big radius is six small radii, six r.
So the linear ratio is one to six. A circumference is a line. So the circumferences are one to six too.
at: the linear ratio is one to six
the circumferences are one to six

slides.say: So each small circumference is a sixth of the big one. Six sixths make a whole. So the six small circumferences together are exactly the big circumference.
The big circumference is easy, two pi r. The radius is nine, and two times nine is eighteen. So it's eighteen pi.
We got eighteen pi again, and we didn't need the small radius at all.
By the way, this is always true. Take circles whose diameters fill the diameter of a big circle. Their circumferences always add up to the big circumference.
It doesn't matter how many circles there are. They don't even need to be the same size.
Why? A circumference is pi times the diameter. The small diameters add up to the big diameter. So pi times them adds up too.
For example, circles with diameters six and twelve sit on a diameter of eighteen. Six pi plus twelve pi is eighteen pi, the big circumference.
at: circles with diameters six and twelve

slides.say: But careful, this is only for circumferences. Each small circle has a sixth of the radius, so a thirty-sixth of the area. Six of them cover only six thirty-sixths, a sixth of the big area.
So the sum of the circumferences is eighteen pi. Choice number four is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number four is our answer
